title: Cyclic Vectors and the Annihilator Ideal of Kⁿ as a K[X]-Module
description: Viewing Kⁿ as a K[X]-module via a matrix M, proves that the module annihilator of Kⁿ is the ideal generated by the minimal polynomial, and that for a cyclic vector v the vector-annihilator ideal {f : f(M)·v = 0} also equals span{minpoly K M}. This is the module-theoretic core behind the invariant-factor / rational-canonical-form decomposition.

overview.historicalContext:
When an n×n matrix M over a field K is fixed, the space Kⁿ becomes a module over the polynomial ring K[X], with X acting as M: a polynomial f acts by f(M). This module-theoretic viewpoint — due to the classical theory of modules over a principal ideal domain — is the engine behind the structure theorems of linear algebra: the invariant factor decomposition and the rational canonical form. Because K[X] is a PID, Kⁿ decomposes as a direct sum of cyclic K[X]-modules K[X]/(d₁) ⊇ ... ⊇ K[X]/(dₖ), where the dᵢ are the invariant factors and dₖ is the minimal polynomial.

The parent entry cayley-hamilton-oq-01 proved the reduction principle f(M) = (f mod minpoly)(M) and that the minimal polynomial generates the annihilator ideal of the whole space. This entry refines the picture to single vectors and cyclic vectors. The annihilator of a single vector v is the ideal of polynomials f with f(M)·v = 0; since K[X] is a PID this ideal is generated by one polynomial, the order (local minimal polynomial) of v. A vector is cyclic exactly when its order has full degree n, in which case its annihilator coincides with the minimal polynomial of M and the cyclic submodule it generates is all of Kⁿ — the situation in which M is similar to a single companion matrix.
overview.problemStatement:
**Open Question (from parent proof cayley-hamilton-oq-01)**: Extend the annihilator theory from the whole space to individual vectors, characterizing when the vector-annihilator ideal equals span{minpoly K M} (the cyclic-vector case underlying the rational canonical form).

**Resolution**: We prove the module annihilator of Kⁿ is span{minpoly K M}; introduce the vector-annihilator ideal vecAnnIdeal M v; show span{minpoly K M} ≤ vecAnnIdeal M v always; and prove equality precisely for a cyclic vector (deg minpoly = n), via monic polynomial division.
overview.text: A 145-line, axiom-free development (2 definitions, 6 theorems) building on Mathlib's Module.AEval' machinery. kn_module_annihilator_eq_minpoly identifies the K[X]-annihilator of Kⁿ with Ideal.span {minpoly K M}, a corollary of Polynomial.span_minpoly_eq_annihilator once minpoly K M is identified with minpoly K M.mulVecLin. vecAnnIdeal M v is the annihilator of the cyclic submodule generated by v, with mem_vecAnnIdeal_iff characterizing membership through the AEval' scalar action. minpoly_mem_vecAnnIdeal and minpoly_ideal_le_vecAnnIdeal give the easy inclusion span{minpoly K M} ≤ vecAnnIdeal M v. The headline cyclic_vecAnnIdeal_eq_minpoly proves the reverse inclusion for a cyclic vector: writing f = q·minpoly + r with deg r < n via modByMonic_add_div, the remainder r kills v (since both f and minpoly do), so IsCyclicVector forces r = 0, i.e. minpoly ∣ f. Monicity of minpoly comes from integrality of M via Cayley-Hamilton (aeval_self_charpoly).
overview.proofStrategy: The crux cyclic_vecAnnIdeal_eq_minpoly proceeds by antisymmetry. The ≥ direction is minpoly_ideal_le_vecAnnIdeal. For ≤: take f ∈ vecAnnIdeal M v, so aeval M.mulVecLin f v = 0 (extracted from the AEval' membership). Reduce 'minpoly ∣ f' to 'f %ₘ minpoly = 0' (modByMonic_eq_zero_iff_dvd, needs monic). Using f = f %ₘ minpoly + minpoly * (f /ₘ minpoly) and aeval(minpoly) = 0, the remainder satisfies aeval M.mulVecLin (f %ₘ minpoly) v = 0; its degree is < n (natDegree_modByMonic_lt with deg minpoly = n), so IsCyclicVector gives r = 0. Monicity of minpoly follows from IsIntegral K M, witnessed by charpoly (Matrix.charpoly_monic, Matrix.aeval_self_charpoly).
keyInsights: Fixing M turns Kⁿ into a K[X]-module; all annihilator statements become ideal statements over the PID K[X].
The minimal polynomial is the generator of the whole-space annihilator; a vector's 'order' (its annihilator generator) divides it and equals it exactly for cyclic vectors.
Cyclicity (no polynomial of degree < n kills v) is exactly what makes the remainder of monic division vanish, upgrading the inclusion span{minpoly} ≤ vecAnnIdeal to equality.
Monicity of the minimal polynomial — needed for polynomial division — comes for free from Cayley-Hamilton, which witnesses integrality of M.

Mathlib's Module.AEval' provides the bridge: the scalar action f • m on the AEval' module corresponds to aeval φ f applied in the base module, letting ideal-theoretic facts transfer to concrete f(M)·v computations.

conclusion.summary: Viewing Kⁿ as a K[X]-module via M, the module annihilator of Kⁿ is span{minpoly K M}, and for a cyclic vector the vector-annihilator ideal coincides with span{minpoly K M}. The cyclic case is proved by monic polynomial division: the remainder of any annihilating polynomial has degree < n and kills v, so cyclicity forces it to vanish. Fully verified, 0 axioms, 0 sorries.
conclusion.implications: This supplies the single-vector annihilator theory underlying the invariant-factor decomposition and the rational canonical form: a cyclic vector generates all of Kⁿ with annihilator exactly the minimal polynomial, the configuration in which M is similar to a companion matrix. It extends the parent entry's whole-space annihilator result to the per-vector level.
